title: How Much of a Model Do We Need? Redundancy and Slimmability in Remote Sensing Foundation Models
claim: Domain-specific models keep nearly full accuracy under aggressive compute reduction, while general-domain baselines degrade sharply at the same budget.
layout: 2 line plots side by side, left-to-right, shaded variance bands, dashed reference line
description: Two line plots share an x-axis, relative compute requirement from 0 to 1. Panel (a) plots relative retention rate on the y-axis. A dark-green curve for remote-sensing foundation models averaged over four datasets stays near 0.86 to 1.0 across the whole range, with a wide shaded band. Yellow, orange and red curves for CV DINOv2 and CV MAE on ImageNet-10 and ImageNet-100 climb steeply from about 0.1 to 0.35 at the lowest compute up to 1.0 at full compute. Panel (b) plots absolute accuracy on m-eurosat. A light-green RS curve with a broad band stays around 0.75 to 0.84. A purple CV MAE curve rises from about 0.58 and crosses a dashed purple line at 0.76 labeled 'CV MAE @ 100% compute'. Legends sit above each panel. The gap between the green and warm-colored curves draws the eye first.
caption: Post-hoc slimmability of RS FMs compared with CV baselines. Legends formatted as: “model(s) @ evaluation data”. a) Relative retention rate: RS FMs across four RS classification datasets maintain on average over 85 % relative accuracy at 1 % compute budget, whereas CV DINOv2 and CV MAE retain on average only 30 % to 35 % on ImageNet-10 and a CV MAE only 12 % on ImageNet-100 at the same compute budget. b) Absolute accuracy on m-eurosat: nine RS FMs (green) retain high accuracy even at 1 % compute budget, matching or exceeding the full-scale CV MAE (dashed line at 0.76). Panopticon is excluded from this comparison because its compute scales differently with width (see Appendix A for details).
abstract: Large-scale foundation models (FMs) in remote sensing (RS) (denoted as RS FMs) are developed following paradigms established in computer vision (CV), yet the validity of transferring CV scaling laws to RS has not been systematically examined. We hypothesize that RS FMs enter an overparameterized regime at substantially smaller scales than their CV counterparts, with task-relevant information encoded redundantly across model dimensions. To test this hypothesis, we apply post-hoc slimmability, uniform width reduction of pretrained encoder transformer blocks, to measure representational redundancy across ten state-of-the-art RS FMs on classification, segmentation, and change detection. RS FMs retain on average over 85% relative accuracy on RS classification datasets under aggressive width reduction, while masked autoencoder (MAE) and DINOv2 pretrained on natural images (denoted as CV MAE and CV DINOv2) degrade sharply on ImageNet subsets of matched class count over the same range of computational requirements. A CV MAE evaluated directly on the same RS dataset narrows but does not close the gap, indicating that both dataset characteristics and domain-specific pretraining contribute to the differences between the models. Analyses of the representation space of the models indicate that task-relevant variance concentrates in few principal components and is redundantly encoded across model dimensions. We further show that learned slimmable training improves over post-hoc slimmability for contrastive objectives, but reconstruction-based objectives do not benefit consistently from current slimmable training protocols. Our findings establish post-hoc slimming as a practical deployment strategy for resource-constrained RS applications and as a diagnostic tool for representational redundancy in RS FMs. Code is available at https://github.com/hackelle/slimmable-remote-sensing-foundation-models.
